newsitem.title: UK: Lonrho shrouded in mist of uncertainties.
newsitem.headline: Lonrho shrouded in mist of uncertainties.

text.p: The haze of uncertainties enveloping Lonrho Plc thickened on Wednesday after a newspaper reported the European Union objected to the link between the British conglomerate and Anglo American.
The Wall Street Journal said the European Commission was set to rule that Anglo's controlling 28 percent stake does not comply with European anti-trust law.
Lonrho declined to comment, saying it was waiting for a statement for the EU, which remained equally tightlipped.

The European Commission has until May 8 to reach a verdict. If it does indeed rule against Anglo, it could strip the South African company of its voting rights, while the mining firm retains its Lonrho shares, one industry watcher said.
The Journal report is just the latest in a string of articles on what might happen to Lonrho, which is in the midst of a protracted overhaul.

The restructuring, laid out over a year ago but amended several times, provides for the sale of Lonrho's hotels business and the divestment of its trading operations. It would leave a Lonrho rump with only the group's extensive mining operations.
But the hotel sale has yet to be completed after the first chain was sold in September and it is unclear how the trading business will be hived off.
Lonrho prefers a demerger, but does not rule out other options.
The split-up process has been covered extensively in the business press including speculation about who is hoping to buy the Princess hotel chain and what other businesses may be sold.
Speculation has been unrelentless and few deals emerged and the architect of Lonrho's break-up plan, German business tycoon Dieter Bock, resigned as chief executive in October.
Bock's exit followed the sale of his Lonrho stake to Anglo American which is particularly interested in the company's mining operations.
But it is Anglo's potential grip on the world platinum market which has sparked the European Commission's probe in December.
The Commission earlier blocked a merger of Lonrho's platinum interests with South Africa's other mining giant, Gencor Ltd. Gencor is appealing to the European Court of Justice.
Lonrho, Anglo and Gencor together control more than 60 percent of the world's output of platinum, which is used in car catalysts to clean up exhaust fumes.
On Wednesday afternoon, Lonrho' shares, which were hit hard by a profit warning last month, stood up one pence on the day to 137p in mid afternoon trade.
Despite the uncertainties, Lonrho shares are worth picking up, some analysts say, citing their belief that prices of some metals, such as platinum, may recover from current weakness.
"They're definitely a 'buy' at the moment even though it may take Lonrho a further six to nine months to sort things out," said analyst Charles Kernot at Paribas Capital Markets.
